prompt: The program below runs to completion. What does it print, and why?

snippets.label: program
snippets.code:
label = "start"
value = 10
if value > 0:
    label = "positive"
if value > 100:
    label = "huge"
print(label)

options.text: It prints positive, because both if statements are evaluated and only the first condition is true.
options.feedback: Correct. label starts as "start", the two if statements are independent, the first condition is true and the second is false, so label is "positive" when it is printed.

options.text: It prints positive, because the first matching if ends the branch and the later if is skipped like an elif.
options.feedback: Half credit. The printed output is correct, but the explanation is not: separate if statements are all evaluated, and here the second condition simply does not match.
options.partial_reason: The printed output is right for this input, but the stated reason is wrong: the later if is not skipped the way an elif is; it is tested on its own and is false here.

options.text: It prints start, because only a literal True or False can control an if statement, so the comparison conditions are not accepted and neither body runs.
options.feedback: An if tests any expression for truthiness. The first condition (value > 0) is true, so label becomes "positive" and is printed; the initial "start" is not what remains.

options.text: It prints huge, because both if bodies run regardless of their conditions, so the last assignment wins.
options.feedback: An if body runs only when its own condition is true. Here value > 100 is false, so the second body is skipped and label stays "positive".

options.text: It prints startpositive, because each assignment adds the new text to the previous value of label, as if using +=.
options.feedback: An ordinary assignment replaces the value rather than adding to it. The first executed assignment sets label to exactly "positive", not "startpositive", and the second if does not run.

explanation: label starts as "start". Both if statements are independent. value is 10, so the first condition (value > 0) is true and label becomes "positive". The second condition (value > 100) is false, so label is not changed. The program prints positive.

verification.rationale: Running the primary snippet with no input writes "positive\n" and exits 0, which supports the correct option: the first condition matches and the second does not, so the initial "start" is replaced once. It does not show that independent if statements can never behave like elif for other inputs, and it does not validate the explanations in the other options.
verification.limitations: One deterministic input only. Rewrite equivalence, asymptotic complexity and whether the half-credit option is genuinely half right are not established by execution.
